life_expectancy.label: Life Expectancy
life_expectancy.summary: Life expectancy demonstrates a strong positive correlation with gross domestic product (GDP), with higher GDP levels generally associated with longer lifespans. Among the regions considered, East Asia exhibits the highest overall life expectancy compared to Southeast Asia and the Pacific. However, it also shows greater internal variation, with an approximate 14-year gap between the highest and lowest values. Mongolia records the lowest average life expectancy in East Asia, at under 70 years, while Hong Kong, Macao, and Japan lead the region with averages between 82 and 84 years. In the Pacific region, the disparity is wider, at around 21 years, with Nauru at just above 60 years and Australia and French Polynesia reaching approximately 82 years. Southeast Asia shows an 18-year range, where Singapore stands out as a high-performing outlier at 82 years, while Myanmar, Timor-Leste, and Laos have lower averages of about 65 years.

birth_rate.label: Birth Rate
birth_rate.summary: Birth rate demonstrates a strong negative correlation with GDP per capita, indicating that higher levels of economic development are generally associated with lower birth rates. Among the regions examined, East Asia records the lowest overall birth rates compared to Southeast Asia and the Pacific. However, it also exhibits notable internal variation, with an approximate difference of 16%, although most countries remain below 12%. Mongolia represents an outlier with the highest birth rate in East Asia at around 23.5%, while Japan and South Korea report the lowest rates, both falling below 8%. In the Pacific region, birth rates are more widely dispersed, with a difference of approximately 19%. Countries such as the Solomon Islands, Nauru, and Vanuatu have higher rates, approaching 32%, whereas Australia, Palau, and New Zealand maintain lower averages near 13%. Similarly, Southeast Asia shows a spread of about 19%, with Timor-Leste exceeding 28% and Singapore remaining below 9%.

fertility_rate.label: Fertility Rate
fertility_rate.summary: Fertility rate, similar to birth rate, exhibits a strong negative correlation with GDP per capita, indicating that as GDP per capita increases, fertility levels tend to decline. Among the regions analyzed, East Asia records the lowest fertility rates compared to Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Despite this, East Asia displays notable internal variation, with an average of approximately 1.5 and a range of about 1.7, though most countries remain below 1.6. Mongolia stands out as an outlier with the highest fertility rate at around 2.7, while Hong Kong reports the lowest at approximately 1.0. In the Pacific region, fertility rates are more widely distributed, with a range of 2.5 and a higher regional average near 3.0; Samoa has the highest rate at over 4.2, whereas Australia records the lowest at 1.8. Southeast Asia has an average fertility rate of 2.3 and the widest variation at 2.9, with Timor-Leste as the highest at 4.1 and Singapore the lowest at 1.2.

population_total.label: Total Population
population_total.summary: There is little to no observable correlation between total population and GDP per capita, indicating that changes in economic output per person do not directly influence overall population size. East Asia has a significantly higher average population compared to Southeast Asia and the Pacific, with an approximate regional average of 260 million, influenced by a major outlier. China represents an extreme case, with a population of around 1.37 billion, while Macao records the lowest at approximately 600 thousand. The Pacific region has the smallest average population, near 2 million, with limited growth over time. Only New Zealand, Australia, and Papua New Guinea exceed 1 million inhabitants, with Australia reaching about 23 million, while many others, such as Tuvalu, remain below 300 thousand. Southeast Asia averages around 57 million, with most countries above 1 million; Brunei is the lowest at 413 thousand, and Indonesia is a high outlier at approximately 257 million.

population_growth.label: Population Growth
population_growth.summary: Similar to total population, population growth demonstrates little to no correlation with GDP per capita, indicating that economic performance does not directly determine growth rates. East Asia records lower average population growth compared to Southeast Asia and the Pacific, with a regional mean of approximately 0.84 and a range of 2.2. Japan is the only country in East Asia experiencing negative growth, at -0.14, while Macao has the highest rate at 2.11. The Pacific region shows greater variability, with an average growth of 0.57 and a wide range of 4.70. Northern Mariana Islands and the Marshall Islands exhibit negative growth, with the former at -1.83, whereas the Solomon Islands records the highest rate at 2.75. Southeast Asia has a higher average growth rate of 1.36 and a narrower range of 1.6, with all countries maintaining positive growth. Timor-Leste has the highest rate at 2.10, while Thailand has the lowest at 0.48.

urban_population_pct.label: Urban Population %
urban_population_pct.summary: Urban population percentage shows a clear positive correlation with GDP per capita, indicating that higher levels of GDP are associated with greater urbanisation. Among the regions analysed, East Asia records the highest average urban population share, followed by the Pacific and then Southeast Asia. All three regions display a general upward trend over time, although the pace of growth appears to have slowed after 2020. East Asia has an average urban population of approximately 82.5%, with a variation of 44.6%; China represents the lower end at 55.4%, while Macao and Hong Kong reach full urbanisation at 100%. The Pacific region has an average of 58.5% but exhibits a wide disparity of 86.5%, ranging from Papua New Guinea at 13.5% to Nauru at 100%. Southeast Asia averages around 50.0%, with a range of 71.1%, where Timor-Leste is the lowest at 28.9% and Singapore the highest at 100%.

school_enrollment_primary.label: Primary School Enrollment
school_enrollment_primary.summary: Primary school enrolment demonstrates a positive correlation with GDP, although the reliability of this relationship may be affected by the presence of null or incomplete data. Overall, higher GDP levels are associated with increased enrolment rates. Across the three regions, values are relatively similar, with Southeast Asia notably maintaining enrolment rates above 100% throughout the 19-year period. East Asia records an average enrolment of 100.9%, with a narrow variation of 5.8%; Hong Kong has the highest average at 104.1%, while Macao has the lowest at 98.4%. The Pacific region shows a higher average of 104.1% but with a wider range of 25.1%, with Vanuatu reaching 119.3%, while New Zealand, Micronesia, and Papua New Guinea fall below 100%. Southeast Asia has the highest regional average at 106.4% and a variation of 26.3%, with Timor-Leste peaking at 122.5%, while Thailand, the Philippines, and Malaysia remain below 100%.

school_enrollment_secondary.label: Secondary School Enrollment
school_enrollment_secondary.summary: Secondary school enrolment, similar to primary enrolment, demonstrates a positive correlation with GDP, although this relationship may be influenced by the presence of incomplete or null data. In general, higher GDP levels are associated with increased enrolment rates. Across the three regions, values are broadly comparable, with Southeast Asia standing out as the only region that does not fall below 100% over the 19-year period. East Asia records an average secondary enrolment of 100.9%, with a relatively small variation of 5.8%; Hong Kong has the highest average at 104.1%, while Macao has the lowest at 98.4%. The Pacific region shows an average of 104.1% with a wider range of 25.1%, where Vanuatu reaches 119.3%, while New Zealand, Micronesia, and Papua New Guinea remain below 100%. Southeast Asia has the highest regional average at 106.4% and a variation of 26.3%, with Timor-Leste peaking at 122.5%, while Thailand, the Philippines, and Malaysia are below 100%.

health_expenditure_per_capita.label: Health Expenditure Per Capita
health_expenditure_per_capita.summary: Health expenditure per capita demonstrates a strong positive correlation with GDP per capita, indicating that higher economic prosperity is associated with increased healthcare spending. Among the regions analysed, East Asia records the highest levels of health expenditure and the most significant growth over the past 19 years, while Southeast Asia shows both the lowest spending and the slowest growth. East Asia has an average health expenditure per capita of approximately 1,625, with a variation of 3,841. Japan records the highest value at 4,015, while Mongolia has the lowest at 174. In the Pacific region, the average stands at 1,004 with a wide range of 5,283, although most countries remain below 1,500. Australia has the highest expenditure at 5,338, whereas Papua New Guinea records the lowest at 55. Southeast Asia averages 379, with most countries below 400 and a range of 2,253. Singapore stands out at 2,295, while Laos and Myanmar remain just above 40.

labor_force_participation.label: Labor Force Participation
labor_force_participation.summary: There is no clear correlation between labour force participation and GDP per capita, indicating that changes in GDP do not significantly influence participation rates. Across all regions, labour force participation generally falls within the 60% to 70% range, with Southeast Asia recording the highest overall levels. East Asia has an average participation rate of approximately 66%, with a relatively narrow variation of 9%. Countries such as Mongolia, Japan, and Hong Kong are at the lower end, around 60%, while China and Macao approach the upper range at just under 70%. In the Pacific, the average participation rate is 61.6%, with a wider disparity of 19.1%. New Zealand records the highest at 68.9%, while Papua New Guinea has the lowest at 49.8%. Southeast Asia shows an average of 67.6% and a broader range of 21.1%, with Cambodia reaching 81.6% and the Philippines at the lower end with 60.5%.

exports_pct_gdp.label: Exports % of GDP
exports_pct_gdp.summary: Exports as a percentage of GDP exhibit a modest positive correlation with GDP, suggesting that increases in GDP are generally accompanied by slight rises in export activity. Among the regions analysed, the Pacific records the lowest export share relative to GDP, while East Asia and Southeast Asia display comparatively similar and higher levels. East Asia has an average export share of 69.1%, with a wide variation of 176.9%. Hong Kong stands out as the only economy exceeding 100%, at 193.6%, whereas Japan records the lowest at 16.7%. In the Pacific region, the average export share is 32.8%, with a narrower range of 60.1%. American Samoa has the highest at 71.9%, while Kiribati has the lowest at 11.8%. Southeast Asia shows an average of 65.2% and a variation of 178.1%, with Singapore exceeding 100% at 193.3%, while Timor-Leste records the lowest at 15.2%.
